title: GA4 advanced and Analytics 360
theme: Design Voltra's GA4 property the right way, use custom definitions, audiences, explorations and attribution settings like an expert, and plan Analytics 360 sub-properties, roll-ups and governance.
jobStory: In this sprint you take ownership of Voltra's analytics. You design the GA4 property: streams, cross-domain, retention, filters and identity. You register custom dimensions, set the attribution rules and build audiences that the media teams use. You answer hard business questions with funnel, path, segment overlap and cohort explorations. Then you plan how Voltra uses Analytics 360 with sub-properties and a roll-up, and you solve a real case where GA4 and the CRM show different booking numbers.
outcomes: I designed and built a GA4 property with cross-domain measurement, 14-month retention, internal traffic filters and unwanted referrals.
I registered custom dimensions and metrics, chose key events, set the attribution model and lookback windows, and built audiences with audience triggers.
I answered business questions with funnel, path, segment overlap and cohort explorations in the GA4 demo account.
I wrote the Analytics 360 plan: sub-properties, a roll-up property, limits, SLA, BigQuery export freshness and access governance.
I found why GA4 and the CRM showed different booking numbers and wrote a fix plan.

tickets.title: Design and build the GA4 property: streams, cross-domain, retention and filters
tickets.goal: Voltra has a written GA4 property design, and you have built and tested the same settings in your own free GA4 property.
tickets.context: Hi, our GA4 was set up by an old agency. Retention is 2 months, our office traffic is counted, and the payment page shows up as a referral source. The accessories store on another domain starts new sessions. Please write the right property design and build it first in a test property, so we can copy the settings safely. - Rahul, Head of Digital
steps: Create a free Google Analytics account for practice: analytics.google.com → Admin → Create → Account `Voltra Practice`, then Property `Voltra - Web - Practice`, time zone `India (GMT+05:30)`, currency `Indian Rupee`.

Create a web data stream: Admin → Data collection and modification → Data streams → Add stream → Web. Use a site you control (a free GitHub Pages site is fine). Keep Enhanced measurement on, but open its settings and turn off `Form interactions` (Voltra will send its own `generate_lead`). Put the Google tag on your site.

Write the design in a Google Doc `Voltra - GA4 property design`: one account for Voltra; one production property for voltra.in plus voltrastore.in (one user journey, so one property); a separate property for the Android/iOS app only if the app team needs its own reporting, else one app stream in the same property; a separate test property for staging. Write the reason for each choice.

Set cross-domain measurement: Admin → Data streams → your web stream → Configure tag settings → Configure your domains. Add both domains (in practice add your site and one second domain or subdomain you own). Write why subdomains of the same domain do not need this setting.

Set unwanted referrals: Configure tag settings → Show more → List unwanted referrals. Add the payment gateway domain (for Voltra the gateway's checkout domain; in practice add `example-pay.com`). Write what goes wrong without it (purchases are credited to the gateway as a referral).

Define internal traffic: Configure tag settings → Show more → Define internal traffic. Add a rule `traffic_type = internal` for your own IP address (search 'what is my IP'). Then Admin → Data collection and modification → Data filters → the Internal Traffic filter: set it to `Testing` first.

Test the filter: visit your site, open Reports → Realtime and add the comparison `Test data filter name` = `Internal Traffic`. When you see your own visits marked, change the filter to `Active`. Write why you test first (an active filter deletes data for ever).

Set data retention: Admin → Data collection and modification → Data retention → Event data retention `14 months`, turn on `Reset user data on new activity`. Write in the doc: retention only limits explorations and other user-level and event-level analysis, not standard reports; Analytics 360 allows up to 50 months; the BigQuery export keeps raw data for as long as you store it.

Check Google signals: Admin → Data collection and modification → Data collection. Write the decision for Voltra (on for remarketing and demographics, with consent mode), and note that signals can add data thresholds to some reports with small user counts.

Check reporting identity: Admin → Data display → Reporting identity. Write the difference between Blended, Observed and Device-based, and which one Voltra uses for daily reporting and which one for a clean comparison with BigQuery.
Link products you will need later (do not link anything that costs money): Admin → Product links → Google Ads links and BigQuery links. Write in the doc which ones the production property needs.
Add a settings table at the end of the doc: setting, value, reason, owner, date checked. This is the checklist for the production property.
acceptance: The practice property has one web stream receiving data (seen in Realtime).
Cross-domain domains, unwanted referrals and an internal traffic rule are set; the internal filter was tested before it was made active.
Event data retention is 14 months.
The design doc explains property and stream choices, Google signals, reporting identity and product links, and ends with a settings table.
evidence: Link to the Google Doc `Voltra - GA4 property design`
Screenshots of: Configure your domains, Data filters (Active), Data retention
Screenshot of Realtime with the `Test data filter name` comparison
hints: If Realtime shows nothing, open your site with Tag Assistant (tagassistant.google.com) to see if the Google tag loads.
Data filters are not retroactive and an active exclude filter cannot be undone for that data.
Retention changes take effect for data going forward; old data that already expired does not come back.

explain.en: In this project I designed Voltra's GA4 property and built the same settings in a practice property. I chose one property for the main site and the store, because it is one customer journey. I set cross-domain measurement, added the payment gateway as an unwanted referral and created an internal traffic filter, which I tested in Realtime before I made it active. I set event data retention to 14 months and explained that it limits explorations, not standard reports. I also documented Google signals, reporting identity and the product links, and finished with a settings checklist for the production property.

vocabulary.en: a source of data for a GA4 property, like a website or an app
keeping one session when a user moves between two of your domains
a domain that GA4 should not count as a traffic source, like a payment page
how long GA4 keeps user-level and event-level data for explorations
how GA4 decides which visits belong to the same user

interview.q: When do you use one GA4 property and when several?
interview.a: I use one property when users move across sites as one journey and the same team owns the data, like Voltra's main site and accessories store. I add separate properties when data must be kept apart for legal or access reasons, or for staging. With Analytics 360 I would rather use sub-properties than many separate tags, because one collection point is easier to govern. The rule is: one journey, one property; separate audiences of users, separate properties.

interview.q: What does data retention change in GA4 and what does it not change?
interview.a: It sets how long user-level and event-level data stays available for explorations and some other analysis. Standard reports use aggregated data and are not limited by it. Standard GA4 offers 2 or 14 months; Analytics 360 offers up to 50 months. For long-term raw data I use the BigQuery export, because there I control the storage.

interview.q: How do you set up an internal traffic filter safely?
interview.a: First I define the internal traffic rule in the web stream with the office IP ranges. Then I set the data filter to Testing and check in Realtime with the test data filter comparison that only internal visits are marked. Only then do I make it Active, because an active filter removes data permanently. I document the IP ranges and review them when offices or VPNs change.

tickets.title: Custom definitions, key events, attribution settings and audiences
tickets.goal: The practice property has the custom definitions and key events from the tracking plan, a documented attribution setup, and audiences the media team can use.
tickets.context: Hi, the media team asks for an audience of people who booked a test ride but did not book online, and they want to report by vehicle model. Also, our dashboards and Google Ads show different conversion numbers and nobody knows which attribution model GA4 uses. Please set this up properly and write it down. - Rahul, Head of Digital
steps: Send test events to your practice property so there is data. In the page source of your test site add, after the Google tag: `gtag('event', 'test_ride_book', {vehicle_model: 'volt_s1', dealer_id: 'D-PUN-014', city: 'pune', value: 1040, currency: 'INR'});` on a button click, and `gtag('event', 'generate_lead', {form_id: 'brochure_form', vehicle_model: 'volt_s1', value: 120, currency: 'INR'});` on a second button.

Turn on debug mode: connect your site in Tag Assistant (tagassistant.google.com), or add `debug_mode: true` to the `gtag('config', ...)` call for this test. Then open Admin → Data display → DebugView, click both buttons and see the events with their parameters.

Register custom dimensions: Admin → Data display → Custom definitions → Create custom dimension. Create event-scoped `Vehicle model` (`vehicle_model`), `Dealer ID` (`dealer_id`), `City` (`city`), `Form ID` (`form_id`). Create a user-scoped `Customer type` (`customer_type`) for later. Write down that data appears only from the time of registration, not before.
Do not register high-cardinality values like `lead_id` as a custom dimension. Write in your notes why (many unique values go into the `(other)` row in reports; use BigQuery for IDs).

Mark key events: Admin → Data display → Events, find `test_ride_book` and `generate_lead`, turn on `Mark as key event`. Then Admin → Data display → Key events → open each one → set the counting method for `generate_lead` (`Once per event` or `Once per session`) and write which one you chose and why.
Set a default key event value for `generate_lead` if no value is sent. Write the value from MKT-103.

Open Admin → Data display → Attribution settings. Write down: the reporting attribution model (choose `Data-driven` or `Paid and organic channels last click`) and the lookback windows: acquisition key events (`first_open`, `first_visit`) 7 or 30 days, all other key events 30, 60 or 90 days. Choose 90 days for Voltra because the median lead-to-booking time is 14 days and the tail is long.

Write a short note `Why GA4 and Google Ads differ` with at least 5 reasons: different attribution models; Google Ads counts by click date while GA4 reports by key event date; Google Ads conversion window vs GA4 lookback; Google Ads can include view-through and modelled conversions; GA4 credits non-Google channels too; counting method differences.

Build audiences: Admin → Data display → Audiences → New audience → Create a custom audience. Audience 1 `Test ride booked - no online booking - 30d`: include users with event `test_ride_book`, exclude users permanently with event `purchase`, membership duration 30 days. Audience 2 `High intent - EMI users`: event `emi_calculator_use` at least 2 times in a session, membership 14 days.

Add an audience trigger to Audience 1: in the audience builder click `Create new` under Audience trigger, event name `audience_test_ride_no_booking`. Write how this event can become a key event or a remarketing signal.

Write the audience notes: audiences need time to fill and are mostly not retroactive, they are shared to linked Google Ads accounts for remarketing only if Google signals or user-provided data and consent allow it, and the standard limit is 100 audiences per property (400 in Analytics 360).
acceptance: DebugView shows both test events with parameters.
Four event-scoped and one user-scoped custom dimension are registered with the exact parameter names.
Two key events are marked with a chosen counting method and a reason.
The attribution model and lookback windows are written with a reason, plus at least 5 reasons why GA4 and Google Ads differ.
Two audiences exist, one with an audience trigger.
evidence: Screenshot of DebugView with `test_ride_book` and its parameters
Screenshot of the Custom definitions list and the Key events list
Screenshot of the audience builder for Audience 1
Link to your notes doc with the attribution decisions
hints: If DebugView is empty, check that Tag Assistant is connected to your site and that you look at the right property.
A custom dimension's parameter name must match the event parameter exactly, including case.
Changes in Attribution settings apply to reports for past and future data, so write the change date in your notes.

explain.en: In this task I set up custom definitions, key events, attribution and audiences in a practice GA4 property. I sent test events with parameters and checked them in DebugView. I registered vehicle model, dealer, city and form as event-scoped dimensions, and I did not register lead IDs because high-cardinality values belong in BigQuery. I marked two key events and chose the counting method. I documented the data-driven model and a 90-day lookback, and listed why GA4 and Google Ads show different numbers. Finally I built two audiences, one with an audience trigger for remarketing.

vocabulary.en: an event or user parameter you register so GA4 reports can show it
how many different values a dimension has
how many days back GA4 looks for touchpoints that get credit
a model that gives credit to touchpoints based on how much they helped convert
an event GA4 creates when a user joins an audience

interview.q: Why do GA4 and Google Ads show different conversion numbers?
interview.a: They use different rules. Google Ads reports by click date and only credits Google Ads clicks, and it can include view-through and modelled conversions. GA4 reports by key event date and shares credit across all channels with its own attribution model and lookback window. The counting method can also differ. I document both setups and use GA4 for cross-channel views and Google Ads for bidding signals.

interview.q: What should not be a custom dimension?
interview.a: IDs and other high-cardinality values like lead IDs, order IDs or timestamps. They push rows into the (other) row and waste the limited slots, which are 50 event-scoped dimensions in standard GA4. I keep those values as event parameters and analyse them in BigQuery. In the GA4 interface I only register dimensions people will group and filter by.

interview.q: How did you choose the lookback window?
interview.a: I looked at the time lag in our funnel. Voltra's median lead-to-booking time is 14 days with a long tail, so a 30-day window would miss real assists. I chose 90 days for non-acquisition key events. I wrote the change date down, because attribution setting changes affect historical reports too.

tickets.title: Answer business questions with GA4 explorations
tickets.goal: You answer four leadership questions with funnel, path, segment overlap and cohort explorations, and you can explain sampling and thresholds.
tickets.context: Hi, before our quarterly review I have four questions: where do online buyers drop off, what do people do just before they buy, how much do our mobile and paid users overlap, and do buyers from the festive season come back. Our own data is still messy, so please use the Google demo account to build the method, then we copy it. - Ananya, CMO
steps: Open the GA4 demo account (Google Merchandise Store, GA4 property). Use the link in the Google Analytics Help article 'Google Analytics demo account'. You get read access; you can create explorations for yourself.

Funnel: Explore → Funnel exploration. Steps: 1 `session_start`, 2 `view_item`, 3 `add_to_cart`, 4 `begin_checkout`, 5 `purchase`. Date range: last 28 days. Keep it a closed funnel first, then switch on `Make open funnel`. Write how the numbers change and why.
In the funnel set Breakdown = `Device category` and turn on `Show elapsed time`. Write the step with the biggest drop on mobile vs desktop and the median time between steps.
Change the visualisation to `Trended funnel` and look for a day where one step drops suddenly. Write what you would check first (release, tag change, payment outage).

Path: Explore → Path exploration → Start over → choose `Ending point` = event `purchase`. Set the node type to `Page title and screen name` for the steps before. Expand 3 steps back. Write the top 3 paths and one surprise.

Segment overlap: Explore → Segment overlap. Build 3 segments: `Mobile users` (Device category = mobile), `Paid traffic` (Session default channel group matches regex `Paid.*`), `Purchasers` (event `purchase`). Write the size of the overlap of all three and what it means for budget decisions.

Cohort: Explore → Cohort exploration. Cohort inclusion `First touch (acquisition date)`, return criteria `purchase`, granularity `Weekly`, metric `Active users` then `Purchase revenue`. Write the week 4 retention for two cohorts.

For each exploration look at the quality icon at the top right. Write if the data is sampled or has thresholds applied. Write the rule: standard GA4 samples explorations above 10 million events per query; Analytics 360 has higher limits (up to 1 billion with 'more detailed results').

Create a segment from the funnel: right-click the `add_to_cart` drop-off for mobile → Create segment from selection. Write how this segment could become an audience (Admin → Audiences) for remarketing.

Put the answers in a Google Slides deck `Voltra - Exploration method` with one slide per question: question, exploration type, settings, screenshot, answer, and what we would do with Voltra's own data.
Add a last slide: which of these four questions you would rather answer in BigQuery and why (cross-session logic, full history, joining CRM data).
acceptance: Four explorations exist: funnel with breakdown and elapsed time, path backwards from purchase, segment overlap with three segments, weekly cohort.
The difference between open and closed funnel is explained with numbers.
Sampling and thresholds are checked and explained for each exploration.
The deck has one slide per question with a clear answer and a next action.
evidence: Link to the Google Slides deck `Voltra - Exploration method`
Screenshots of the four explorations with their settings panels visible
hints: In a closed funnel users must enter at step 1. In an open funnel they can enter at any step.
If you see a red or orange quality icon, shorten the date range or remove a high-cardinality dimension.
Path exploration 'Start over' is needed to set an ending point.

explain.en: In this task I answered four leadership questions with GA4 explorations in the demo account. I built a funnel from session start to purchase, compared closed and open funnels, and broke it down by device with elapsed time. I used a path exploration backwards from purchase, a segment overlap of mobile, paid and buyers, and a weekly cohort of returning buyers. For each one I checked sampling and thresholds and explained the limits of standard GA4 and Analytics 360. I put the method in a deck so we can repeat it on Voltra's own data.

vocabulary.en: a GA4 analysis tool for deeper questions than standard reports
a funnel where users must start at the first step
a group of users who share a start date or a start event
using only part of the data to answer faster
GA4 hides rows with few users to protect privacy

interview.q: When do you use an open funnel instead of a closed funnel?
interview.a: I use a closed funnel when I want the true journey from a defined entry, like session start to purchase. I use an open funnel when users can enter at any step, for example landing directly on a product page from an ad. Comparing the two shows how many users skip early steps. For Voltra's booking flow I report the closed funnel and use the open one to find entry points.

interview.q: How do you handle sampling and thresholds in GA4?
interview.a: I check the quality icon on every exploration. For sampling I shorten the date range or move the question to BigQuery, and with Analytics 360 I can use more detailed results with a much higher limit. Thresholds come from privacy rules when user counts are small, often with Google signals on. I can change reporting identity to device-based for a check, or use BigQuery, which has no thresholds.

interview.q: Which questions do you take out of GA4 and into BigQuery?
interview.a: Questions that need full history beyond retention, custom session logic, exact counts or joins with CRM data. For example, which campaigns bring test rides that later turn into deliveries needs CRM data, so it belongs in BigQuery. GA4 explorations are great for fast discovery. BigQuery is where I build the trusted, repeatable version.

tickets.title: Write the Analytics 360 plan: sub-properties, roll-up, limits and governance
tickets.goal: Leadership has a clear plan for how Voltra uses Analytics 360: property structure, sub-properties, a roll-up, the limits and SLA we pay for, BigQuery export, and who can see what.
tickets.context: Hi, we signed Analytics 360 this year, but we use it exactly like the free version. The export team must not see India dealer data, the agencies must not see revenue, and the board wants one global view. Please write how we should use 360, and be honest about what it does and does not give us. - Ananya, CMO
steps: Learn first (free): take the GA4 learning path on Skillshop (skillshop.withgoogle.com, search 'Google Analytics') and read the Analytics 360 help pages on sub-properties and roll-up properties. You do not need a 360 licence to write this plan.

Create a Google Doc `Voltra - Analytics 360 plan` with headings: What 360 adds, Property structure, Sub-properties, Roll-up property, Limits we need, BigQuery export, Access and data restrictions, Change process, Costs and risks.

Under What 360 adds make a table, standard vs 360, with: data retention (14 vs up to 50 months), custom dimensions (50/25 event/user vs 125/100), custom metrics (50 vs 125), key events (30 vs 50), audiences (100 vs 400), event parameters per event (25 vs 100), exploration sampling limit (10 million vs up to 1 billion events), daily BigQuery export (1 million events per day vs much higher), fresher daily export and faster data freshness, sub-properties and roll-ups (360 only), SLA for collection, processing and reporting (360 only). Mark each row with how Voltra uses it.

Under Property structure draw: one 360 source property `Voltra - Global` (voltra.in, voltrastore.in, export sites, app); sub-properties `Voltra - India D2C`, `Voltra - Exports`, `Voltra - Dealer network`; one roll-up property `Voltra - Board view` that combines the global property with a separate property of a future brand.

Under Sub-properties write the filter for each one (for example `Exports` = events where `country` is not India, or stream = export site) and that a sub-property receives data from the time it is created, has its own settings and access, and its events count toward billing.

Under Roll-up property write when it is right (combine several source properties for a group view) and its limits (it only contains data from its creation, some features differ from normal properties, and its events also count toward billing). Write why you do not use a roll-up for Voltra's main site (one source property is better).

Under BigQuery export write: daily export of the source property and the sub-properties to separate datasets, fresh daily export for 360 so tables arrive early in the morning, streaming export only where an intraday need is real (streaming has a cost in BigQuery), dataset location in India region `asia-south1` if data residency matters.

Under Access and data restrictions define roles per group: Administrator (MarTech lead, 2 people), Editor (analytics team), Marketer (media team: can edit audiences, key events and attribution), Analyst (agency analysts), Viewer (management). Add data restrictions: `No cost metrics` and `No revenue metrics` for agency users. Grant access at the sub-property level where possible.

Under Change process write the rules: changes to key events, attribution settings, retention and filters need a ticket and approval by the MarTech lead; every change is written in a change log with date; use the Admin → Property change history to audit.
Under Costs and risks write honestly: 360 is billed by event volume, sub-properties and roll-ups add billable events, the SLA only helps if we report incidents, and 360 does not fix bad tagging.
Finish with a one-page summary and a 90-day rollout plan (week by week).
acceptance: The standard vs 360 table has at least 10 correct rows and says how Voltra uses each one.
The structure shows one source property, at least 3 sub-properties with filters, and a roll-up with a clear reason.
Access roles and data restrictions are defined per user group.
Costs and risks are stated honestly, and there is a 90-day rollout plan.
evidence: Link to the Google Doc `Voltra - Analytics 360 plan`
Screenshot or link of your structure diagram
Screenshot of your Skillshop progress or certificate (free)
hints: Check every limit in the official help pages. Limits change; write the date you checked them.
A sub-property is for splitting one property; a roll-up is for combining several properties.
Data restrictions hide cost and revenue metrics from roles that should not see them.

explain.en: In this task I wrote Voltra's Analytics 360 plan. I compared standard GA4 and 360 in a table: retention, custom dimensions, key events, audiences, sampling limits, BigQuery export, sub-properties, roll-ups and the SLA. I designed one global source property with sub-properties for India D2C, exports and dealers, and a roll-up only for a board view across brands. I defined access roles and data restrictions so agencies cannot see revenue. I was honest that 360 is billed by events and does not fix bad tagging, and I added a 90-day rollout plan.

vocabulary.en: the paid enterprise version of Google Analytics with higher limits and an SLA
a 360 property that gets a filtered part of a source property's data
a 360 property that combines data from several source properties
service level agreement: a promise about data freshness and uptime
a setting that hides cost or revenue metrics from some users

interview.q: What does Analytics 360 give you that the free GA4 does not?
interview.a: Sub-properties and roll-up properties, much higher limits for custom dimensions, audiences, key events and retention up to 50 months, and higher exploration limits. It also gives a much higher daily BigQuery export limit, a fresher daily export and an SLA for collection and processing. It does not make bad tracking good, so I still need a clean tracking plan. I justify 360 with the governance and scale it gives, not with features we will not use.

interview.q: When would you use a sub-property and when a roll-up?
interview.a: A sub-property splits one source property, for example to give the export team only export data with its own access and settings. A roll-up combines several source properties, for example a board view across two brands. Both only have data from the time they are created, and both add billable events. For Voltra's main site I keep one source property and use sub-properties for access control.

interview.q: How do you govern access to analytics at a company with many agencies?
interview.a: I give the lowest role that lets each group do its job and grant it at the sub-property level where possible. Agencies get Analyst or Marketer roles with no cost and no revenue metrics if contracts require it. Important settings like key events and attribution need a ticket and approval. I review access every quarter and remove people who left.

tickets.title: Case: booking numbers differ between GA4 and the CRM
tickets.goal: You explain the gap between GA4 purchase events and CRM bookings with numbers, split it into causes, and write a fix plan with owners.
tickets.context: Hi, finance asked why GA4 shows 2,410 online bookings last month while the CRM shows 3,050 paid bookings. On some days GA4 is even higher than the CRM. The board sees both numbers. Please find out what is going on and tell me which number to trust for what. - Ananya, CMO
steps: First finish the practice lab: open Practice → Funnel detective (`cro-funnel`) in this app and solve it. It trains the method you need here: find the leaking step and the segment, and separate tracking problems from real behaviour.
Create a Google Sheet `Case MKT-205 - GA4 vs CRM bookings` with tabs `CRM`, `GA4`, `Match`, `Causes`.

Build practice data in `CRM`: 30 rows with columns `booking_id`, `paid_at` (date and time in UTC), `channel`, `status` (`paid`, `cancelled`, `test`), `payment_method` (`upi`, `card`, `netbanking`). Make 3 rows `test`, 2 rows `cancelled`, and 4 rows paid just before midnight IST.

Build practice data in `GA4` the way a GA4 exploration would export it: Explore → Free form, rows `Transaction ID` and `Date`, metric `Purchases` (or event count of `purchase`). In your data: 20 transaction IDs that match the CRM, 2 IDs that appear twice, 1 row with `(not set)`. Do the same exploration once in the GA4 demo account and write how many transaction IDs appear more than once.
In `Match` use `=COUNTIF(GA4!A:A, A2)` for each CRM booking to see if GA4 has it, and the reverse for each GA4 ID. Mark every row: matched, missing in GA4, duplicate in GA4, extra in GA4.
Explain the time zone effect: the CRM stores UTC and GA4 reports in the property time zone (IST, UTC+5:30). Convert `paid_at` to IST and recount by day. Write how many bookings move to another day.

Write in `Causes` the size of each cause in your data: test bookings, cancellations, time zone, duplicate `purchase` events (thank-you page reload or back button), users who pay by UPI in another app and never return to the thank-you page, consent denied or ad blockers, missing `transaction_id`.

Check the tag side in GTM Preview on your practice site (or describe it from the `cro-gtm` lab): does `purchase` fire on a page view of `/booking/thank-you` (fires again on reload) or on a dataLayer event pushed once after payment success? Write which one is safer.

Write the fix plan: send `purchase` only once per `transaction_id` (set a flag in session storage or fire from the server); send missing purchases from the payment webhook with the Measurement Protocol, using the stored `client_id` and `session_id`; exclude test bookings with a parameter; keep consent mode on and accept that some gap remains.

Write the rule for which number to trust: CRM for finance and board reporting of bookings; GA4 for channel mix, funnel and behaviour; report the match rate (GA4 matched / CRM paid) every week as a tracking health KPI with a target, for example above 85%.
Write a one-page summary for the CMO: the gap, the causes with numbers, the fix plan with owners and dates, and the trust rule.
acceptance: The lab `cro-funnel` is solved in the app.
Every CRM and GA4 row is classified (matched, missing, duplicate, extra).
The gap is split into named causes with a number for each, including time zone and duplicates.
The fix plan has owners and dates and includes a server-side or Measurement Protocol solution for missing purchases.
A weekly match-rate KPI with a target is defined.
evidence: Link to the Google Sheet `Case MKT-205 - GA4 vs CRM bookings`
Screenshot of the demo account exploration with Transaction ID
The one-page summary for the CMO
hints: A gap in both directions (GA4 lower on most days, higher on some) usually means two causes at once: lost events and duplicates.
UPI payments often finish in another app. Many users never come back to the browser tab.
GA4 is not a finance system. Do not try to make it match the CRM to 100%.

explain.en: In this case I found why GA4 and the CRM showed different booking numbers. First I solved the funnel lab to practise the method. Then I matched GA4 transaction IDs with CRM booking IDs and classified each row as matched, missing, duplicate or extra. I found several causes: test and cancelled bookings, UTC versus IST dates, duplicate purchase events from page reloads, and UPI users who never returned to the thank-you page. I wrote a fix plan with a once-only purchase event and server-side events from the payment webhook. I also set a rule: the CRM is the truth for finance, GA4 is for channels and funnels, and we track the match rate every week.

vocabulary.en: a unique ID for each order or booking, used to match systems
the share of CRM orders that GA4 also recorded
a way to send events to GA4 from a server

interview.q: GA4 and the CRM show different order numbers. How do you investigate?
interview.a: I start with a row-level match on transaction ID, not with totals, because totals hide causes that cancel each other out. Then I classify rows as matched, missing, duplicate or extra and put a number on each cause. Typical causes are time zones, test and cancelled orders, duplicate purchase events, users who never reach the thank-you page and consent or ad blockers. I fix what is fixable and report a match rate for the rest.

interview.q: How do you stop duplicate purchase events?
interview.a: I fire purchase on a dataLayer event that the site pushes once after payment success, not on a thank-you page view. On the client side I also store the transaction ID in session storage and skip the tag if it was already sent. The strongest solution is to send it from the server when the payment webhook arrives. I check duplicates every week in BigQuery by counting purchases per transaction ID.

interview.q: Which number do you give the board?
interview.a: For bookings and revenue I give the CRM or finance number, because it is the system of record. I use GA4 to explain where bookings come from and how users behave, and I say clearly that it is a sample with known loss. I also show the match rate as a tracking health number. That way nobody argues about which tool is right; each number has its job.
